claim: EAG-like (ELK) voltage-gated potassium channels are abundantly expressed in the brain.
source: EAG-like (ELK) voltage-gated potassium channels are abundantly expressed in the brain.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract without specific experimental data in this manuscript, but is presented as established knowledge.

claim: VDP manifests as a potentiation of current amplitude, hyperpolarizing shift in voltage sensitivity, and slowing of deactivation in response to a depolarizing prepulse.
source: VDP manifests as a potentiation of current amplitude, hyperpolarizing shift in voltage sensitivity, and slowing of deactivation in response to a depolarizing prepulse.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the experimental observations presented in the manuscript, supported by data in Figures 1B-D.

claim: VDP of D. rerio ELK channels involves the structural interaction between the intracellular N-terminal eag domain and C-terminal CNBHD.
source: Here we show that VDP of D. rerio ELK channels involves the structural interaction between the intracellular N-terminal eag domain and C-terminal CNBHD.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by deletion experiments (Figure 3A-C), mutation experiments (Figure 3D-F), and tmFRET measurements (Figures 5-6).

claim: There is a rearrangement in the eag domain-CNBHD interaction with the kinetics, voltage-dependence, and ATP-dependence of VDP.
source: Combining transition metal ion FRET, patch-clamp fluorometry, and incorporation of a fluorescent noncanonical amino acid, we show that there is a rearrangement in the eag domain-CNBHD interaction with the kinetics, voltage-dependence, and ATP-dependence of VDP.
evidence: This is supported by tmFRET experiments showing changes in fluorescence with voltage (Figure 5E-H), ATP/Mg2+ dependence (Figure 5A-B), and kinetic measurements (Figure 6A-C).

claim: The activation of ELK channels involves a slow open-state dependent rearrangement of the direct interaction between the eag domain and CNBHD, which stabilizes the opening of the channel.
source: We propose that the activation of ELK channels involves a slow open-state dependent rearrangement of the direct interaction between the eag domain and CNBHD, which stabilizes the opening of the channel.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental data and kinetic modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: ERG channels (Kv11) constitute the fast delayed rectifier in cardiomyocytes and are partly responsible for the repolarization of the cardiac action potential.
source: ERG channels (Kv11) constitute the fast delayed rectifier in cardiomyocytes and are partly responsible for the repolarization of the cardiac action potential (Sanguinetti et al., 1995; Trudeau et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: EAG channels (Kv10) and ELK channels (Kv12) are abundantly and almost exclusively expressed in the brain where they also regulate electrical excitability.
source: EAG channels (Kv10) and ELK channels (Kv12) are abundantly and almost exclusively expressed in the brain where they also regulate electrical excitability, though their precise physiological function is not well understood (Shi et al., 1998; Warmke and Ganetzky, 1994; Zou et al., 2003; Saganich et al., 2001; Martin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Genetic deletion of ELK channels was shown to cause hippocampal hyperexcitability and epilepsy in mice.
source: Genetic deletion of ELK channels was shown to cause hippocampal hyperexcitability and epilepsy in mice (Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: EAG channels are also abundantly expressed in many forms of cancer.
source: In addition, EAG channels are also abundantly expressed in many forms of cancer (Camacho, 2006; Pardo and StuhmerStühmer, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: KCNH channels are composed of four subunits around a centrally located pore, where each subunit contains six transmembrane segments and an intracellular N-terminal and C-terminal region.
source: Like other voltage-gated potassium channels, KCNH channels are composed of four subunits around a centrally located pore, where each subunit contains six transmembrane segments and an intracellular N-terminal and C-terminal region (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about KCNH channels, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: KCNH channels do not bind and are not directly regulated by cyclic nucleotides, including cAMP and cGMP.
source: Although the KCNH channels contain a cyclic nucleotide-binding homology domain (CNBHD) in the C-terminal region, the channels do not bind and are not directly regulated by cyclic nucleotides, including cAMP and cGMP (Brelidze et al., 2009; Robertson et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The analogous cyclic nucleotide-binding pocket of the CNBHD is occupied by an 'intrinsic ligand' from a short sequence at the C-terminal end of the CNBHD.
source: Instead, the analogous cyclic nucleotide-binding pocket of the CNBHD is occupied by an 'intrinsic ligand' from a short sequence at the C-terminal end of the CNBHD (Marques-Carvalho et al., 2012; Brelidze et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The intrinsic ligand regulates KCNH channel function.
source: This intrinsic ligand regulates KCNH channel function (Marques-Carvalho et al., 2012; Brelidze et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2017) and explains, in part, why KCNH channels are not regulated by cyclic nucleotides.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: There is an interaction between the N-terminal eag domain (PAS domain and PAS cap) and C-terminal CNBHD in KCNH channels.
source: Another important structural feature of KCNH channels is the interaction between the N-terminal eag domain (PAS domain and PAS cap) and C-terminal CNBHD (Gianulis et al., 2013; Gustina and Trudeau, 2009; Haitin et al., 2013; Whicher and MacKinnon, 2016) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The eag domain-CNBHD interaction has been demonstrated to be critical for the proper function of KCNH channels.
source: This interaction has been demonstrated to be critical for the proper function of KCNH channels.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent statement about mutations and their effects.

claim: Mutations in KCNH channels that impair the eag domain-CNBHD interaction lead to alterations in channel trafficking and gating.
source: Mutations in KCNH channels that impair this eag domain-CNBHD interaction lead to alterations in channel trafficking and gating, which are thought to underlie some forms of Long QT Syndrome and cancer (Curran et al., 1995; Gustina and Trudeau, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The activation of zELK channels at depolarizing voltages exhibits prominent double exponential kinetics, with a fast (~4 ms) and a slow (~200 ms) component.
source: The first is that the activation of zELK channels at depolarizing voltages exhibits prominent double exponential kinetics, with a fast (~4 ms) and a slow (~200 ms) component (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Prolonged depolarization causes the zELK channel to transition to a second more stable open conformation.
source: This suggests that prolonged depolarization is causing the channel to transition to a second more stable open conformation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the double exponential kinetics observed.

claim: A depolarizing prepulse to +60 mV caused about a −60 mV shift in the G-V curve to more hyperpolarized voltages as well as a dramatic increase in the peak tail-current amplitude.
source: The depolarizing prepulse caused about a −60 mV shift in the G-V curve to more hyperpolarized voltages as well as a dramatic increase in the peak tail-current amplitude (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The tail current amplitude increased 3.5 ± 0.3 fold (n = 11) for depolarizing voltage pulses of longer durations.
source: The tail current amplitude increased 3.5 ± 0.3 fold (n = 11) for depolarizing voltage pulses of longer durations, with a time course that closely matched the slow component of the activation kinetics (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is directly measured from experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The time constant of the tail current increased from 8.4 ± 0.4 ms to 16.9 ± 1.5 ms with longer pulses (n = 12).
source: More interestingly, the time constant of the tail current increased from 8.4 ± 0.4 ms to 16.9 ± 1.5 ms with longer pulses (n = 12) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is directly measured from experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Channels closed more slowly from a potentiated open state.
source: This suggests that channels closed more slowly from a potentiated open state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the increased time constant of tail currents with longer depolarizing pulses.

claim: A simple kinetic scheme with a slow transition to a potentiated mode can quantitatively account for the double exponential activation, the shift in the G-V curve with depolarizing prepulses, and the slowing of the tail currents with longer depolarizing pulses.
source: While clearly oversimplified, this simple gating scheme could quantitatively account for the double exponential activation (Figure 1F), the shift in the G-V curve with depolarizing prepulses (Figure 1G), and the slowing of the tail currents with longer depolarizing pulses (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulated data in Figures 1F-H matching the experimental observations.

claim: zELK channels exhibit a dramatic run-up in activity after patch excision.
source: zELK channels exhibit a dramatic run-up in activity after patch excision.
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The run-up manifested as a 2.2 ± 0.3 fold increase in tail current amplitude compared to the cell-attached configuration (measured after +120 mV depolarization, n = 7).
source: Similar to VDP, this run-up manifested as an increase in tail current amplitude (a 2.2 ± 0.3 fold increase compared to the cell-attached configuration, measured after +120 mV depolarization, n = 7) (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is directly measured from experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The run-up manifested as a significant shift of the G-V curve of channel activation to more hyperpolarized voltages (V1/2 = −52.5 ± 3.5 mV, n = 6).
source: and a significant shift of the G-V curve of channel activation to more hyperpolarized voltages (V1/2 = −52.5 ± 3.5 mV, n = 6) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is directly measured from experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The shift of the G-V curve happened gradually after excision and reached steady-state after about 20 mins.
source: The shift of the G-V curve happened gradually after excision and reached steady-state after about 20 mins (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The VDP was almost completely eliminated in excised patches, with no further shift in the G-V curve with depolarizing prepulses.
source: Interestingly, the VDP was almost completely eliminated in excised patches, with no further shift in the G-V curve with depolarizing prepulses (Figure 2C), and no slowing of the tail currents with longer depolarizing pulses (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figures 2C-E.

claim: Patch excision shifted the channels into the potentiated mode even without a depolarizing prepulse.
source: This suggests that patch excision shifted the channels into the potentiated mode even without a depolarizing prepulse.
evidence: This is an inference based on the elimination of VDP after patch excision.

claim: Patch excision revealed a prominent voltage-dependent inactivation in zELK channels, particularly at very depolarized voltages (>+60 mV).
source: Patch excision also revealed a prominent voltage-dependent inactivation in zELK channels, particularly at very depolarized voltages (>+60 mV) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Patch cramming was able to completely restore the cell-attached channel behavior within five mins.
source: Patch cramming, i.e. inserting the excised patch back into the intracellular regions of the oocyte, was able to completely restore the cell-attached channel behavior within five mins, indicating some cytosolic factors were lost in the inside-out configuration (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figures 2A and B.

claim: Some cytosolic factors were lost in the inside-out configuration.
source: Patch cramming, i.e. inserting the excised patch back into the intracellular regions of the oocyte, was able to completely restore the cell-attached channel behavior within five mins, indicating some cytosolic factors were lost in the inside-out configuration (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the patch cramming experiment restoring channel behavior.

claim: Reducing reagent DTT in the bath did not prevent the run-up, suggesting disulfide bonding was not involved in this run-up.
source: Reducing reagent DTT in the bath did not prevent the run-up, suggesting disulfide bonding was not involved in this run-up (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Supplementation of the bath solution with 2 mM ATP/Mg2+ was able to prevent the run-up and maintain the VDP observed in the cell-attached configuration.
source: We found that supplementation of the bath solution with 2 mM ATP/Mg2+ was able to prevent the run-up and maintain the VDP observed in the cell-attached configuration (Figure 2F,G and H).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figures 2F-H.

claim: ATP alone without Mg2+ was not able to prevent the run-up.
source: ATP alone without Mg2+ was not able to prevent the run-up (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 is required for VDP in zELK.
source: These results suggest that, consistent with previous findings in human ELK1 (Li et al., 2015), PI(4,5)P2 is also required for VDP in zELK, and hydrolysis of PI(4,5)P2 after patch excision leaves the channel in a potentiated state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ATP/Mg2+ dependence and comparison with previous literature.

claim: Hydrolysis of PI(4,5)P2 after patch excision leaves the channel in a potentiated state.
source: These results suggest that, consistent with previous findings in human ELK1 (Li et al., 2015), PI(4,5)P2 is also required for VDP in zELK, and hydrolysis of PI(4,5)P2 after patch excision leaves the channel in a potentiated state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ATP/Mg2+ dependence and comparison with previous literature.

claim: The VDP was almost completely abolished in zELK channels with the eag domain deleted (zELK Δeag).
source: We found the VDP was almost completely abolished in zELK channels with the eag domain deleted (zELK Δeag) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In the cell-attached configuration, the average change in V1/2 (ΔV1/2) with a +60 mV prepulse was −12.7 ± 1.4 mV (n = 7) for zELK Δeag compared to −54.0 ± 2.0 mV (n = 14) in wild-type zELK.
source: In the cell-attached configuration; the average change in V1/2 (ΔV1/2) with a +60 mV prepulse was −12.7 ± 1.4 mV (n = 7) (Figure 3B) compared to −54.0 ± 2.0 mV (n = 14) in wild-type zELK.
evidence: This is directly measured from experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: zELK Δeag did not show an increase in the time constant of deactivation with longer depolarizing pulses.
source: In addition, zELK Δeag did not show an increase in the time constant of deactivation with longer depolarizing pulses (Figure 3C) as seen in the wild-type channel.
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Charge reversal mutations (zELK-R57D or D681R) that would disrupt the salt bridge not only shifted the initial V1/2, but also attenuated the VDP.
source: We found that charge reversal mutations (zELK-R57D or D681R) that would disrupt the salt bridge not only shifted the initial V1/2, but also attenuated the VDP (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figures 3E and F.

claim: Charge-swapping mutations (zELK-R57D, D681R) partially rescued the channel behavior to that of the wild-type channels.
source: When we made the charge-swapping mutations (zELK-R57D, D681R) by combining the individual reversal mutations, we partially rescued the channel behavior to that of the wild-type channels (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figures 3E and F.

claim: The eag domain and CNBHD are interacting via the salt bridge and this interaction is supporting the VDP.
source: These results indicate that the eag domain and CNBHD are interacting via the salt bridge and this interaction is supporting the VDP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutation experiments showing that disrupting the salt bridge attenuates VDP.

claim: Wild-type mouse EAG1 channels do not have VDP.
source: Wild-type mouse EAG1 channels do not have VDP (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figures 3G and H.

claim: The mEAG1-zELK chimera exhibited prominent VDP.
source: However, the mEAG1-zELK chimera exhibited prominent VDP (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The average ΔV1/2 with the +60 mV prepulse was −39.1 ± 2.6 mV (n = 9) for the mEAG1-zELK chimera in the cell-attached configuration.
source: The average ΔV1/2 with the +60 mV prepulse was −39.1 ± 2.6 mV (n = 9) for the mEAG1-zELK chimera in the cell-attached configuration.
evidence: This is directly measured from experimental data.

claim: The eag domain-CNBHD complex of zELK is sufficient to confer VDP on mEAG1.
source: These results suggest that the eag domain-CNBHD complex of zELK is sufficient to confer VDP on mEAG1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the chimera experiments showing that replacing the intracellular domains of mEAG1 with those from zELK confers VDP.

claim: tmFRET measures the FRET between a donor fluorophore and a nonfluorescent transition metal ion acceptor.
source: tmFRET measures the FRET between a donor fluorophore and a nonfluorescent transition metal ion acceptor (Latt et al., 1972; Horrocks et al., 1975; Richmond et al., 2000; Sandtner et al., 2007; Taraska et al., 2009a, 2009b).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the tmFRET technique, supported by citations.

claim: The efficiency of tmFRET is steeply dependent on the distance between the donor fluorophore and the acceptor metal ion.
source: The efficiency of tmFRET is steeply dependent on the distance between the donor fluorophore and the acceptor metal ion and can be directly measured from the percent quenching of the donor's fluorescence upon addition of the metal ion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the tmFRET technique.

claim: tmFRET measures much shorter distances (10–20 Å) compared to traditional FRET and has less orientation dependence.
source: Compared to traditional FRET, tmFRET measures much shorter distances (10–20 Å) and has less orientation dependence, making it ideal for measuring intramolecular distances in proteins (Taraska et al., 2009a).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the tmFRET technique, supported by a citation.

claim: L-Anap was site-specifically incorporated into zELK channels using the amber (TAG) stop-codon suppression strategy.
source: L-Anap was site-specifically incorporated into zELK channels using the amber (TAG) stop-codon suppression strategy (Chatterjee et al., 2013; Kalstrup and Blunck, 2013; Aman et al., 2016; Sakata et al., 2016; Zagotta et al., 2016).
evidence: This is the method used in the study, supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The emission spectrum of L-Anap overlaps with the absorption spectrum of Co2+-dihistidine, predicting a distance for 50% FRET efficiency (R0) of 12 Å.
source: The emission spectrum of L-Anap overlaps with the absorption spectrum of Co2+-dihistidine, predicting a distance for 50% FRET efficiency (R0) of 12 Å (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) (Zagotta et al., 2016; Aman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is calculated based on spectral overlap shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and supported by citations.

claim: Only patches from oocytes injected with all three components (zELK-E51TAG-YFP mRNA, L-Anap, and pANAP plasmid) exhibited Anap fluorescence.
source: Only patches from oocytes injected with all three components exhibited Anap fluorescence (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The linear correlation between the Anap fluorescence and the YFP fluorescence and current in the patches indicates that virtually all of the Anap fluorescence was coming from L-Anap incorporated within the functional channel.
source: The linear correlation between the Anap fluorescence and the YFP fluorescence and current in the patches indicates that virtually all of the Anap fluorescence was coming from L-Anap incorporated within the functional channel and not from any nonspecific background fluorescence (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figures 4D and E.

claim: With an increasing concentration of Co2+ applied to the intracellular face of excised patches held at −100 mV, the Anap fluorescence decreased monotonically.
source: With an increasing concentration of Co2+ applied to the intracellular face of excised patches held at −100 mV, the Anap fluorescence decreased monotonically (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The Co2+-mediated quenching was reversed by applying 10 mM EDTA to chelate the divalent cations.
source: The Co2+-mediated quenching was reversed by applying 10 mM EDTA to chelate the divalent cations (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The quenching of Anap fluorescence by Co2+ is indicative of FRET between the L-Anap and the bound Co2+.
source: This quenching of Anap fluorescence by Co2+ is indicative of FRET between the L-Anap and the bound Co2+.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed quenching and its reversal by EDTA.

claim: The channel without the dihistidine produced only a small amount of quenching up to 1 mM Co2+.
source: The channel without the dihistidine produced only a small amount of quenching up to 1 mM Co2+ (Figure 5A) and was used to correct the FRET efficiency for any quenching that was not due to Co2+ binding to the dihistidine (see tmFRET efficiency calculation in the Materials and methods) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The apparent tmFRET efficiency increased with increasing Co2+ concentration and was well described by a Langmuir isotherm with an apparent affinity of around 70 µM, and a maximal FRET efficiency of 0.71 ± 0.05 (n = 4).
source: The apparent tmFRET efficiency increased with increasing Co2+ concentration and was well described by a Langmuir isotherm with an apparent affinity of around 70 µM, and a maximal FRET efficiency of 0.71 ± 0.05 (n = 4).
evidence: This is directly measured from experimental data and fitted with a Langmuir isotherm.

claim: Co2+ binding to the dihistidine in the CNBHD is in close proximity to L-Anap in the eag domain.
source: These results suggest that Co2+ binding to the dihistidine in the CNBHD is in close proximity to L-Anap in the eag domain, as predicted from the X-ray crystal and cryoEM structures (Haitin et al., 2013; Whicher and MacKinnon, 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the high FRET efficiency observed, consistent with structural predictions.

claim: zELK-E51Anap, K729H-E733H channels behaved similarly to wild-type zELK channels and exhibited VDP in ATP/Mg2+.
source: zELK-E51Anap, K729H-E733H channels behaved similarly to wild-type zELK channels and exhibited VDP in ATP/Mg2+ (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In the presence of ATP/Mg2+, zELK-E51, K729H-E733H channels exhibited a shift in the G-V curve (ΔV1/2) of −43.5 ± 2.7 mV with depolarizing prepulses.
source: In the presence of ATP/Mg2+, zELK-E51, K729H-E733H channels exhibited a shift in the G-V curve (ΔV1/2) of −43.5 ± 2.7 mV with depolarizing prepulses, only slightly less than the wild-type channel in the cell-attached configuration (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is directly measured from experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: With ATP/Mg2+ added to the bath, the FRET efficiency at −100 mV decreased to 0.46 ± 0.08 (n = 4) compared to 0.71 ± 0.05 without 2 mM ATP/Mg2+ added.
source: We found that, with ATP/Mg2+ added to the bath, the FRET efficiency at −100 mV decreased to 0.46 ± 0.08 (n = 4) compared to 0.71 ± 0.05 without 2 mM ATP/Mg2+ added (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is directly measured from experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Using the Förster equation and an R0 of 12 Å, the change in FRET efficiency corresponds to a distance change of 2.0 Å.
source: Using the Förster equation and an R0 of 12 Å, this corresponds to a distance change of 2.0 Å.
evidence: This is calculated from the measured FRET efficiencies using the Förster equation.

claim: At hyperpolarizing voltages, the two sites within the eag domain and CNBHD are further apart when the channel is not potentiated and closer together when the channel is potentiated.
source: These results suggest that, at hyperpolarizing voltages, these two sites within the eag domain and CNBHD are further apart when the channel is not potentiated and closer together when the channel is potentiated.
evidence: This is an inference based on the FRET efficiency measurements with and without ATP/Mg2+.

claim: The steady-state Anap fluorescence intensity with 1 mM Co2+ decreased at +120 mV compared to −100 mV.
source: With patch-clamp fluorometry, we found the steady-state Anap fluorescence intensity with 1 mM Co2+ decreased at +120 mV compared to −100 mV (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figures 5E and F.

claim: The decrease in fluorescence was not present without dihistidine or in the absence of ATP/Mg2+.
source: This decrease was not present without dihistidine or in the absence of ATP/Mg2+ (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The wavelength of the L-Anap peak emission was not significantly shifted despite the reduction in the intensity of peak emission produced by the +120 mV voltage pulse in the presence of 1 mM Co2+.
source: We found the wavelength of the L-Anap peak emission was not significantly shifted despite the reduction in the intensity of peak emission produced by the +120 mV voltage pulse in the presence of 1 mM Co2+ (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: This is directly observed in the spectral data shown in Figures 5G and H.

claim: The decreased fluorescence is consistent with a FRET mechanism for Co2+ quenching and not a change in environment.
source: Together with the absence of a fluorescence change without a dihistidine (Figure 5F), these results are consistent with a FRET mechanism for Co2+ quenching and not a change in environment (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: This is an inference based on the spectral data and control experiments.

claim: Membrane depolarization causes a ATP/Mg2+-dependent and voltage-dependent rearrangement between the eag domain and CNBHD.
source: These results indicate that, similar to VDP, membrane depolarization causes a ATP/Mg2+-dependent and voltage-dependent rearrangement between the eag domain and CNBHD.
evidence: This is an inference based on the voltage-dependent changes in FRET observed.

claim: The rearrangement between the eag domain and the CNBHD is associated with VDP.
source: This suggests that the rearrangement between the eag domain and the CNBHD is associated with VDP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between FRET changes and VDP properties.

claim: In the presence of ATP/Mg2+ and 1 mM Co2+, the Anap fluorescence decreased with a +60 mV depolarization and recovered after repolarization to −100 mV.
source: In the presence of ATP/Mg2+ and 1 mM Co2+, the Anap fluorescence decreased with a +60 mV depolarization and recovered after repolarization to −100 mV (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The time constant, 261 ± 56 ms, for the decrease in Anap fluorescence was not statistically different from the time constant of approximately 308 ± 26 ms for the slow component of channel activation associated with the development of VDP.
source: The time constant, 261 ± 56 ms, for the decrease in Anap fluorescence was not statistically different from the time constant of approximately 308 ± 26 ms for the slow component of channel activation associated with the development of VDP (Figure 6A and B, also Figure 1D).
evidence: This is directly measured from experimental data and compared statistically.

claim: In the absence of ATP/Mg2+, the channel activated quickly with the +60 mV depolarization without a slow component, and the concurrent Anap fluorescence was unchanged by the voltage step.
source: In the absence of ATP/Mg2+, the channel activated quickly with the +60 mV depolarization without a slow component, and the concurrent Anap fluorescence was unchanged by the voltage step (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The time constant for recovery of the Anap fluorescence at −100 mV was 137.5 ± 16 ms.
source: The time constant for recovery of the Anap fluorescence at −100 mV was 137.5 ± 16 ms (Figure 6A and C).
evidence: This is directly measured from experimental data shown in Figures 6A and C.

claim: With an increased duration of the −100 mV pulse, the VDP gradually disappeared; a 500 ms recovery pulse shifted the V1/2 back to the control value without the +60 mV prepulse.
source: With an increased duration of the −100 mV pulse, the VDP gradually disappeared; a 500 ms recovery pulse shifted the V1/2 back to the control value without the +60 mV prepulse (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The time constant of the V1/2 recovery of wild-type channels was not significantly different from the time constant of the recovery of Anap fluorescence.
source: The time constant of the V1/2 recovery of wild-type channels was not significantly different from the time constant of the recovery of Anap fluorescence (p>0.05, Figure 6C).
evidence: This is directly measured and compared statistically.

claim: There is a rearrangement between the eag domain and CNBHD that exhibits the same ATP/Mg2+-dependence, voltage-dependence, and kinetics as VDP.
source: Overall these tmFRET experiments demonstrate that there is a rearrangement between the eag domain and CNBHD that exhibits the same ATP/Mg2+-dependence, voltage-dependence, and kinetics as VDP.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the tmFRET experiments presented.

claim: The VDP is produced partially or fully by a slow open-state dependent rearrangement of the direct interaction between the eag domain and CNBHD, which stabilizes the opening of the channel.
source: Combined with our finding that VDP is altered or eliminated by mutations of the eag domain and CNBHD (Figure 3), these experiments suggest that the VDP is produced partially or fully by a slow open-state dependent rearrangement of the direct interaction between the eag domain and CNBHD, which stabilizes the opening of the channel.
evidence: This is the main mechanistic conclusion of the study, based on the combined evidence from mutations and tmFRET experiments.

claim: hELK1 is downregulated by PI(4,5)P2.
source: Previously, it has been shown that hELK1 is downregulated by PI(4,5)P2 (Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: For both hELK1 and zELK, PI(4,5)P2 degradation leaves the channels in a potentiated mode that no longer undergoes VDP.
